  • Completes production deployments in about five minutes

  • Absorbs traffic spikes without additional capacity provisioning

  • Reduced serverless spend by 90% with Fluid compute

  • Updates doctor- and patient-facing applications independently

OpenEvidencehelps physicians find medical evidence during care, whether they’re checking a dosage on intensive care rounds or handling a case outside their specialty without a specialist nearby. Answers draw on peer-reviewed literature and include citations, so doctors can examine the sources behind them.

OpenEvidence’s small team began using Vercel to get early experiments online and kept that workflow as the product grew, relying on the platform to handle web deployments and capacity.

Building software physicians depend on

The stakes are different when software helps inform medical decisions. An incorrect answer can affect how a doctor treats a patient, while an unavailable application can cut off access to evidence when it is needed.

OpenEvidence supportedmore than 20 million clinical consultations in January 2026. The company also reported thatmore than 100 million Americans were treated by doctors using OpenEvidence in 2025.

"Honestly, life or death is not inaccurate," says Kush Khosla, Engineering Lead at OpenEvidence. "We operate in situations where it's an ER and they really need to know what's going on. Uptime is very, very important to us."

"A lot of doctors and medical professionals are used to really outdated software," says Andy Yoon, Engineering Lead at OpenEvidence. A more modern experience still needs to meet physicians' expectations of speed, stability, clarity, and information they can trust. The small team needs a way to test updates to the web application before putting them into production and to roll back if something goes wrong.

Keeping releases simple as the audience grows

Andy recalls why Vercel suited the team he joined at OpenEvidence. "I was pretty much the only engineer on our team coming from an actual frontend background," he says. "Most of our team works in Python and machine learning." He adds, "Given the makeup of our engineering team, Vercel really scaled with our needs so well."

The team builds its physician-facing web application with theNext.js framework. When engineers push changes to a development branch, Vercelbuilds and deploys a preview, giving them a link they can use for live demos and share with colleagues to try new features. Pushing or merging into the production branch then triggers the production build and deployment. If a release needs reverting, the team canroll back to a previous deployment.

That workflow lets the team release multiple times a day, with each change becoming available to a physician audience that Kush thinks about whenever he ships something:

More doctors without more provisioning

Keeping that application available means handling demand the team can’t always anticipate. Andy was scrolling through Slack when he saw the message that OpenEvidence had gone viral on TikTok, reaching around two million views in under a week. He watched traffic climb and checked the logs.Response times stayed fast and error rates remained near zero, and with no additional capacity to provision, he went back to his work.

Beyond sudden spikes, the team has accommodated sustained growth without rebuilding the web application.

"Not once have I had to think, now that we have five times as many doctors, what's happening to page loads or time to first paint," Kush says. "The scaling has happened so naturally that we end up focusing on other things."

A 90% drop in serverless spend

As usage grew, VP of Engineering Micah Smith was watching compute costs. The team enabledFluid computefor its functions on Vercel, and Micahdescribed the resultalongside the wider infrastructure budget:

"We reduced our serverless spend by 90% while maintaining the same performance, and even as we've scaled up to 1000x growth, Vercel is less than 5% of our overall infra spend."

Fluid compute lets multiple requests share a running function instance, so it can handle other work while a request waits for another service, such as a database or an AI backend, to respond. WithActive CPU pricing, that waiting time doesn’t incur CPU charges, though memory remains billed while requests are in progress.

A familiar workflow for a new audience

Take Home, OpenEvidence’s first patient-facing application, lets a doctor translate a clinical answer into plain language and share it with a patient, who logs in to review and save the evidence. Clinical-trial matching is also part of the application’s planned direction.

To support this expansion, the team uses a pattern established through dozens of early proofs of concept, each deployed as its ownVercel projectwith a custom domain. Stakeholders could open those applications and test the workflows for themselves. Getting new projects online in minutes helped the team find product-market fit and made it easier to win early enterprise partnerships.

Take Home has its own project and domain too, so engineers can update the patient experience without deploying the other applications.

With Take Home, evidence that helps a doctor during a consultation can become something a patient returns to afterward.

item.title: Introducing Vercel Security Review
item.content:encoded:
Today, we are launchingVercel Security Reviewin public beta.

Security Review is a new capability inVercel Agent, alongside Code Review and Investigation. Once enabled, it scans for vulnerabilities on every push to a team's connected GitHub repositories.

Findings appear as comments on pull requests, are listed in the Security dashboard, and are available via CLI. With your permission, Vercel Agent can also validate and push fixes for findings.

How it works

Security reviews are triggered by GitHub push events, including direct pushes to your production branch. In monorepos, reviews are scoped to the project's root directory. Here is how it works:

  1. You push code to a GitHub repository connected to a Vercel project.

  2. As soon as the push lands, Security Review scans the changed code for vulnerabilities like missing authorization checks or exposed secrets.

  3. Findings are posted to the Security dashboard. On private and internal repositories, Security Review also adds a GitHub check to the commit and comments on the pull request.

  4. You can fix findings by clickingFix with Vercel Agentin the dashboard, or use the CLI to pull findings and have your own coding agent implement changes.

  5. When subsequent security reviews no longer detect a finding, it is marked as no longer detected in the dashboard, and the GitHub comment is closed.

Each review compares the push against a base and covers only what changed. For deployments, the base is the branch’s previous deployment, so the agent reviews the change against what’s already running. Because it only scans the diff, Security Review finishes in seconds and can run on every preview and production deployment.

What the agent checks

The agent reads the diff along with the surrounding code, traces how the changed code can be reached, checks for existing protections, and rechecks each finding before reporting it. That process is how it catches logic flaws like missing authorization checks, which pattern-matching scanners miss.

Each review also applies your team’ssecurity policies, which you can write in plain language and apply to specific projects or across your team. For example, a policy can require any endpoint that returns customer data to check that the requester owns it. You can also manage policies with the Vercel CLI, usingvercel security policy.

How findings are tracked

Each new finding is checked against ones that have already been reported, so the same issue isn’t flagged twice. Every finding is tied to the deployment where it first appeared and changes are followed from there. That means that when a vulnerable change from a pull request is merged into your production branch, the finding is flagged in production as well.

When a later review no longer detects the issue in an environment, the agent marks the finding as no longer detected there.

Acting on findings

Every finding explains the vulnerability and how to fix it, with links to the commit and deployment where it first appeared.

Findings are listed in theVulnerability viewin the Security dashboard, where you can ask Vercel Agent to validate and commit fixes. Findings are alsoavailable via CLI, so you can fix vulnerabilities with your own coding agent.

Each new finding generates an audit log event, which Enterprise teams can send to their SIEM throughAudit Log Drains.

Here is a demo of sample findings in the dashboard:

Fixing vulnerabilities with Vercel Agent

When Vercel Agent can fix a finding, you will see the option to clickFix with Vercel Agenton the finding page in the dashboard. After you click, the agent confirms the vulnerability still exists, then makes the smallest change that fixes it and updates the tests.

Say a developer pushes a change to an invoice download endpoint, and the lookup doesn't check which organization the invoice belongs to. Within seconds, Security Review flags that any signed-in user could download another organization's invoice by changing its ID. Vercel Agent's fix scopes the lookup to the user's organization:

Fixing vulnerabilities with your own coding agent

You can point your coding agent or other systems at the Vercel CLI to pull and fix vulnerabilities:

Findings in the dashboard also give you the ability to copy detailsas Markdown or JSON, making it easy to paste them into an agent conversation.

Every code change needs security review

Frontier AI models are making vulnerabilities far easier to find and exploit. Last month, researchers turned two decade-old flaws in PHP core intoworking remote code execution exploitswith relatively little effort.

At the same time, agents are writing more of the code teams ship, and each handles security review its own way, or in many cases, not at all.

With Vercel Security Review, you can scan every push on every project for vulnerabilities by default, using the security policies you set.

What's next

Security Review starts with code pushed to GitHub. Next, we're bringing it to deployments from the Vercel CLI and v0, and to repositories that don't deploy on Vercel. We're also working on suggested fixes you can apply directly from the pull request.

Get started

Vercel Security Review is available today in public beta for Pro and Enterprise teams.

To get started, enable Security Review inVercel Agent Settings. You can choose to run Security Review on all projects, or only the ones you choose. To learn more, read theChangelog entryand theSecurity Review documentation.

Security Review is billed at theVercel Agent rate, with model tokens at the provider's rate and no markup, plus $0.25 per million tokens.

item.title: Introducing Geist Serif
item.content:encoded:
Geist started as a monospace typeface for developers, built for the editors and terminals where they spend their day doing their work. From there it grew into Geist Sans for product interfaces, and then into Geist Pixel, which was inspired by the grids of early computer screens.

Today, we're adding a new member to the family:Geist Serif.

Geist Serif is a high-contrast display serif built on the same foundations as Geist Sans, Geist Mono, and Geist Pixel. It has fine, saw-toothed serifs and sharp hairlines, and it was drawn to communicate messages powerfully both in the physical world and on the high-density screens on modern devices.

Same system, new voice

At Vercel, Geist Sans runs the product. For headlines, though, we wanted a second voice, one that belongs to the same system, instead of a stranger picked from a drop-down menu.

A lot of tech brands have moved away from clean sans-serifs to get some personality back, and many of them borrow from vintage computer ads. Geist Serif takes a different path: toward fashion, editorial design, and magazine headlines. It's our homage to the artists behindRolling StoneandHarper's Bazaar.

From the beginning, each Geist family has read from a chapter of type history: the Swiss design movement, early terminal and DOS computing, and now editorial print.

Display first

Geist Serif began as a set of sketches byEvil Rabbit, which Andrés Briganti then expanded. The first letters already showed an expressive serif, in the spirit of typefaces like Victor Serif and Stanley.

When Mark Davis took over the drawings, we made the first release a display face for headlines, posters, and other large sizes, while work on the full family continued. Print has always struggled to hold fine hairlines and sharp serifs, but today's displays can handle a high level of detail. We wanted the new face to take full advantage of modern screens, so we thinned every downstroke by 50% and tightened the sidebearings to push the contrast as far as it would go.

Each serif has a wedge on one side and a curve on the other, so the proportions are classical and look beautiful in print, but the construction is new and optimized for digital devices.

From the first prototype to today

The first prototype of Geist Serif was shared on April 1, 2026. Here's the same word, Geist, in that prototype, compared with the display drawing shipping today.

Geist grew teeth

The goal was to honor our original intent and keep the serif closely tied to the sans, even when the letters sit on top of each other. Geist Serif’s stems match Geist Sans, and the two share widths and postures.

The saw-toothed serifs and high contrast give Geist an editorial voice. One phrase kept coming up as each character was drawn: “Geist grew teeth.”

Four families, one x-height

Geist Serif uses the same cap height and x-height as Geist Sans, so you can drop it into any Geist layout without moving a line. Mix Sans, Mono, Pixel, and Serif in the same sentence and every word looks the same size.

Four variants, one axis

Like Geist Pixel, Geist Serif has a variable axis that swaps the shape of every dot in the font, including those oniandjand in punctuation. The axis is called Element Shape (ELSH), and it gives you four variants: Regular with round dots (the default), Square, Triangle (a nod to the Vercel logo), and Heart.

Each variant also ships as its own static file. If you use the variable font, pick a variant withfont-variation-settings:

Crafted by hand

In July the font had227 glyphs. It now has894and covers 352 Latin-script languages, and we worked through more than 52,000 kerning pairs to get the spacing right. Some of the details are tiny. The eye of theg, for example, is tilted exactly 7°.

Specs at a glance

Geist Serif ships with:

  • 1 weight (Regular)

  • 4 variants (Regular, Square, Triangle, Heart)

  • 894 glyphs

  • 5 stylistic sets (ss01toss05)

  • 352 supported languages

Getting started

Geist Serif ships in the same package as the rest of the family:

Exports and CSS variables:

  • GeistSerif(variable, all shapes): --font-geist-serif

  • GeistSerifRegular: --font-geist-serif-regular

  • GeistSerifSquare: --font-geist-serif-square

  • GeistSerifTriangle: --font-geist-serif-triangle

  • GeistSerifHeart: --font-geist-serif-heart

Each one has its own entry point, so you only ship the font file you use. For example, inlayout.tsxwithGeistSerifRegular:

You can also download the font files, test every stylistic set, and inspect each glyph atvercel.com/font.

What’s next

Regular is the first style we’re releasing, and the rest of the family is already in progress. We’re testing future versions while building this one, so this release is just the start.

Weights from Thin to Black

The variable font will range from Thin (100) to Black (900). In this week’s proofs, the g in Black is the letter we can’t stop looking at.

Toward a text face

To explore a text version, we built a foundry tool that measures strokes, including where they meet, and thickens the display outlines. It edits the outlines directly, so we can set real words and see which strokes need more weight.

Italics, built rule by rule

We’re also developing an italic generated entirely in Python. We slanted existing italics back upright and compared them with their romans. With the angle removed, the remaining differences show up clearly, and we turned them into rules we can test and revise. This italic won’t be the final version, but breaking glyphs in code helps us find the limits faster.

More scripts and Google Fonts

Cyrillic support is planned to match Geist Sans and Geist Mono, and Geist Serif will come to Google Fonts after launch.

One family

With Geist Sans, Geist Mono, Geist Pixel, and now Geist Serif, the family runs from UI text and code to expressive display type, and all four feel at home together.

item.title: Simplifying runtime caching on Vercel
item.content:encoded:
Today, we’re bringing Data Cache into Runtime Cache, giving developers one product for data caching across frameworks and APIs. If you use Next.jsfetchcaching orunstable_cache, you won’t need to change your code. Pro and Enterprise projects will get larger storage allocations.

Runtime Cache lets your code reuse fetched or computed data across requests without operating a separate caching service. Over the past year, we’ve improved read performance during traffic bursts, increased storage budgets, and made cache usage easier to investigate.

Why we built Runtime Cache

Data Cache was originally launched as Vercel’s data caching service for the Next.js App Router, used byfetchcaching andunstable_cache. UnlikeCDN caching, which stores complete HTTP responses, Data Cache stores data your application uses to generate those responses. A product page, for example, can reuse cached catalog data while rendering a personalized response for each visitor.

We wanted developers to have access to that service without depending on Next.js. Last year, weintroduced Runtime Cachewith a direct API:getCachefrom@vercel/functions. Applications can use it for feature flag lookups in Routing Middleware, caching CMS content during builds, and data caching in SvelteKit and Nuxt apps.

Frameworks can expose this service through their own APIs, too. On Vercel, Next.js itself uses the Runtime Cache API for'use cache: remote', which caches function and component outputs.

How Runtime Cache works

The infrastructure behind Runtime Cache is a distributed caching service shared by many teams. A Go API handles requests, backed by Redis fleets in every Vercel region. Every hour, the service handles more than 440 million reads and moves more than 18 TB of data.

Each region has its own cache. A cache hit takes one round trip to the cache service in the region where your code runs. Vercel handles authentication with short-lived credentials, so you don’t need to manage API keys.

On a cache miss, your app or framework fetches or computes the value and writes it to that region’s cache. The service doesn’t check other regions for a cached copy.

Each cached entry stores its tags and write time. When the service reads an entry, it checks a separate tag store in the same region for those tags’ invalidation timestamps. If any tag was invalidated after the entry was written, the entry is stale.

For example, an application can tag all its cached product data withcatalog. When the catalog changes, invalidating that tag writes a single timestamp, even if a million entries share the tag. The service doesn’t need to find and delete those entries individually.

The invalidation immediately updates the tag store in the region receiving the request. Vercel’s shared tag infrastructure, also used by theCDN, distributes the timestamp through the global push pipeline, typically reaching other regions within a few hundred milliseconds.

Your app or framework chooses what to cache and handles misses. Runtime Cache handles regional storage, authentication, and distributing tag invalidations across regions.

What we’ve shipped

Faster reads during traffic bursts

Checking whether an entry is still fresh adds a dependency to every cache hit. During traffic bursts, a slow shard in the tag store could delay reads even when the cached value was already available.

We added circuit breakers that let reads temporarily check freshness using tag timestamps cached in memory, so they can proceed without waiting for the slow shard to respond. During this fallback, a read can briefly treat recently invalidated data as fresh.

We enabled the breakers in every region in August. During the heaviest bursts in our largest region, p99 cache-service read latency fell to about one fifth of its previous level at comparable traffic. On-call alerts for this failure mode stopped.

More storage and fewer evictions

We raised Runtime Cache storage budgets for Pro projects in June and Enterprise projects in October, giving applications more room for data they reuse. This reduces the need to evict cached entries to make room for new data. Among Enterprise projects with frequent evictions, cache miss rates roughly halved within a day.

More visibility into cache behavior

We’ve added deployment markers, revalidation causes, and write utilization to the Runtime Cache view inObservability. These help you compare changes in cache behavior with releases, see why entries are refreshed, and identify data that gets written to the cache but rarely read.

Bringing Data Cache into Runtime Cache

We’re simplifying caching on Vercel by consolidating on Runtime Cache. Until now, Next.jsfetchcaching andunstable_cachehave used Data Cache, whilegetCacheand'use cache: remote'have used Runtime Cache. The migration brings all four APIs under Runtime Cache, so you and coding agents have one set of storage budgets and usage tools to work with.

If you usefetchcaching orunstable_cache, nothing changes in your code. On Pro, each project and environment gets its own storage allocation, with 8x the space of Data Cache’s previous team-wide pool. Enterprise projects get 10x their previous Data Cache storage.

Previously unbilled Data Cache reads and writes will followRuntime Cache pricing. New teams use Runtime Cache automatically, and existing teams will receive their migration and billing details in advance.

See thechangelogfor the rollout, pricing, and early opt-in details. Before migrating, review your cache usage and follow theoptimization guideto reduce unnecessary reads and writes.

item.title: Vercel Flags starts 7x faster and no longer extends function duration
item.content:encoded:
On Vercel, theVercel FlagsSDK now initializes faster on cold starts, and usage reporting no longer keeps functions running after the response.

Faster cold starts

Two changes speed up SDK initialization on cold starts:

  • The SDK loads and parses the flags datafile bundled with your deployment as soon as the client is created, so it’s ready before your code evaluates its first flag.

  • Every function invocation now includes the current datafile revision, so the SDK can check whether the bundled datafile is up to date without a network request.

In internal testing, eliminating the network wait reduced p75 cold-start SDK initialization time from over 70 ms to 10 ms, roughly 7x faster.

After initialization, flag reads are effectively instant. Across cold and warm invocations, p99 flag-read latency is under 1 ms.

Usage reporting no longer extends function duration

The SDK previously usedwaitUntilfor usage reporting, keeping functions running after the response was sent. It now passes usage events to the Vercel runtime, so reporting no longer adds to function duration.

item.title: Introducing Virtual Models on AI Gateway
item.content:encoded:
Today, we are introducingVirtual ModelsonAI Gateway.

Virtual Models are an abstraction of the model string and configurations your apps and developers use. With a single virtual model ID, you can change and update models, configure fallbacks and priority, and enforce Zero Data Retention centrally. The virtual model configuration applies wherever the ID is used.

Assign a virtual model ID to an agent task, and pass it as the model string wherever that task is called. You can then change the model and settings behind the virtual model ID in AI Gateway, and your apps and agents will pick up the new configuration automatically, without code changes or redeploys.

New models use the same virtual model ID

In the last 90 days, 125 new models from more than 10 labs became available on AI Gateway. That adds up to about 10 a week. AI Gateway already makes switching a one-line change. You call any of those models by ID, and AI Gateway routes each request to a healthy provider and can fall back to others when one fails.

That one line still lives in your code, so switching usually means a redeploy.

Virtual Models move model selection and configuration to AI Gateway. You create an ID for a task, likevmc/coding-agent, and then configure the model and the settings it should use:

You can then use that virtual model ID as the model string wherever the task runs:

Forcoding agentslikeClaude Code,Codex, and others, connect them withvercel ai-gateway setup, then select your virtual model in each harness's model picker or configuration.

When a different model is available, including one from another provider,edit the virtual model. Every app and agent that callsvmc/coding-agentpicks it up within a few minutes, with no code change or deployment needed:

Give each task its own model

An agent task like support ticket triage can run hundreds of times an hour and needs to be cheap. Other tasks, like legal contract review, may only run a few times a day, but require a high level of reasoning.

You can now give each task a purpose-built virtual model and easily evolve that model and configuration over time:

Settings such as fallbacks, Zero Data Retention, and tags stay with the virtual model when you switch models. Provider options apply per provider, so an Anthropic-specific setting stops applying when you point the virtual model at an OpenAI model. Review your provider options whenever you switch providers.

Before you switch a virtual model that serves production traffic, point a second one, likevmc/coding-agent-candidate, at the new model and run your evals against it. If quality drops after the switch, point the original back at the previous model.

Govern which models your team uses and how

Anyone on your team can call a virtual model, and team roles control who can make changes to it. Platform and security teams can centrally govern and test models and settings, while still easily giving teams access to new models as they are released.

Settings on a virtual model win over the same settings in a request, so callers can't override the provider order, fallbacks, or service tier you chose. For example, you can configure the fallback models forvmc/storefront-assistantcentrally, and every app using that virtual model ID will use the same failover configuration, even if a request specifies different fallbacks.

If a virtual model requires Zero Data Retention or providers that don't train on request data, those configurations are enforced even if a request explicitly setszeroDataRetentionordisallowPromptTrainingto false.

Tags on a virtual model replace any tags sent with the request, so spend lands on the task no matter how each app tags its calls. TheVirtual Models pageshows requests, spend, and success rate for each task.

item.title: Introducing Vercel CI
item.content:encoded:
Coding agents are opening more pull requests than ever, and each one waits on CI before anyone can review or merge it. Most CI systems run the entire workflow on every push, even a one-line change. The more your agents push, the more time you spend waiting on CI.

Today, we're announcing Vercel CI in Beta. It runs only the tasks affected by your code change, and spins up only the compute those checks need, the same wayFluid computescales with your traffic.

At Vercel, our CI now keeps up with our coding agents. Time fromgit pushto "CI passed" is2-6x fasterthan it was before.

How it works

Vercel CI uses Turborepo to understand your tasks and which ones depend on each other. It readsturbo.json, so if you're already using Turborepo, there's no separate CI config to write.

If you're not on Turborepo yet, addturbo.jsonand theturbopackage. It works in single-package repos too.

Then tag the tasks you want Vercel CI to run.

"tags": ["ci"]is all you need to get started. No workflow YAML to maintain, no drift between your CI config andturbo.json, and Remote Cache is on by default.

When you or your agent push code, Vercel CI determines which tasks need to run based on the change. Tasks whose inputs haven't changed come from cache. The remaining tasks each run on their own machine, powered byHive, Vercel's compute layer, and start as soon as their dependencies finish.

Vercel CI gives each task the compute it needs and nothing more.

Running your CI on Vercel

To get started, follow thedocumentationor prompt your agent from your repo:

Once set up, you or your agent can watch and inspect CI through theVercel dashboard,Vercel CLI, orVercel MCP. When something fails, go straight to the failing task, see what's blocked behind it, and open its logs, or search across recent runs to see whether a test has been flaky all week.

Vercel CI posts a check to your pull request on GitHub, so your existing branch protection rules can block merges on failure, the same way they do today.

Closing the loop

Vercel CI has already completed nearly 8 million tasks across our own repositories and the private beta, and we're just getting started. We're working to keep shrinking the time between writing code and running it in production.

As we work toward general availability, we plan to add:

  • Advanced observability

item.title: PostgreSQL 19 Released
item.content:encoded:
PostgreSQL 19 Released

Most years PostgreSQL ships a new release in September, but this year's release came two months later thanks mainly to the flurry of issues that the PostgreSQL team needed to address as part of the ongoing AI-reported vulnerability apocalypse.

This release was definitely worth the wait. My favorite new feature is this one:

For applications that send reads to standbys, PostgreSQL 19 adds "read-your-writes" consistency with the new WAIT FOR LSN command. A session on a standby can use WAIT FOR LSN to wait until the standby has replayed the write-ahead log (WAL) up to a specific log sequence number (LSN) before running a query, so the application can read data it just wrote on the primary.

In practice, that looks like this:

UPDATE movie SET genre = 'Dramatic' WHERE genre = 'Drama';
        SELECT pg_current_wal_insert_lsn();

That returns a value like 0/0306EE20. Store that somewhere (a signed cookie would work) such that on a subsequent request your application can do:

WAIT FOR LSN '0/0306EE20' WITH (TIMEOUT '0.1s');
        SELECT * FROM movie WHERE genre = 'Drama';

The timeout is optional - if you provide one you'll get an error if the replica you are talking to doesn't catch up within the specified time.

I first encountered this pattern in Wikipedia, which has a hand-rolled version of this built against MySQL replication:

In addition to this, MediaWiki attempts to ensure that the user sees events occurring on the wiki in chronological order. A few seconds of lag can be tolerated, as long as the user sees a consistent picture from subsequent requests. This is done by saving the primary binlog position in the session, and then at the start of each request, waiting for the replica to catch up to that position before doing any reads from it.

Here's the relevant MediaWiki code, which these days uses MySQL's WAIT_FOR_EXECUTED_GTID_SET() function and falls back to SOURCE_POS_WAIT().

Via Lobste.rs

External sandboxes for coding agents
item.content:encoded:
External sandboxes for coding agents

I've been exploring new ways to sandbox code that is executed by agents, with a focus on making it safer to try out local models without worrying that a mistake or prompt injection attack might cause them to take damaging actions on a machine.

I worked on this project with Prime Radiant, the AI research lab behind Superpowers and other projects.

My post on the Prime Radiant blog introduces the external sandbox pattern, where code executed by the agent runs inside a dedicated sandbox while the agent itself lives outside of that sandbox.

To demonstrate this pattern we've released three sandbox server implementations:

  • external-sandbox-v86 runs a Node.js server which then uses v86 to run Alpine Linux inside WebAssembly.
  • external-sandbox-container is a Python web server which runs the sandbox in Alpine Linux inside an Apple Containers instance.
  • external-sandbox-quicksand is another Python web server, this time using Microsoft's Quicksand sandboxing library, which bundles QEMU and Alpine Linux in a Python package!

Each of these implementations offers the same localhost API. You can then configure Pi, Claude Code, or Codex to send API calls to that sandbox any time they want to execute code.

The sandboxes also include an optional HTTP/HTTPS allow-list proxy, so you can control exactly which hosts your agent's code is allowed to communicate with - plus a credential replacement mechanism to make authenticated API calls without sharing a secret with the agent. Here's the UI you can use to reconfigure that proxy while the sandbox is still running:

I continue to be fascinated by the challenge of safely running untrusted code. This external sandbox pattern provides a neat way to experiment with different approaches.

item.title: Running the full server-side Datasette Python app in the browser with service workers and Pyodide
item.content:encoded:
Datasette Lite is my port of the Datasette Python application to run directly in the browser using WebAssembly and Pyodide. I've released a complete rewrite of Datasette Lite using service workers, and it's now almost indistinguishable from the real server-side application.

You can now do all of the following, using a carefully crafted URL to lite.datasette.io:

  • Load client-side Datasette to browse any SQLite database, JSON file, CSV file or SQL script
  • Select a released version of Datasette to load from PyPI
  • Load a specific commit, tag, or branch name from the Datasette GitHub repository
  • Pick from over 100 versions of SQLite to use with Datasette
  • Install additional Datasette plugins from PyPI or URLs to wheel files, including JavaScript visualization tools

The ability to load specific Datasette references, plugins, and SQLite versions makes this a fantastic tool for linking to demos of work-in-progress features or bug reproductions, without needing to spin up a full web server to serve that demo.

As an example, consider the following URL:

https://lite.datasette.io/?install=datasette-maplibre&url=https://gist.githubusercontent.com/simonw/39fa5d399465766039549912e2b3d291/raw/f6dfba99a75cbb8b5d9386223220eb52272767ee/demo.db&metadata=https://gist.githubusercontent.com/simonw/39fa5d399465766039549912e2b3d291/raw/f6dfba99a75cbb8b5d9386223220eb52272767ee/metadata.yml#/demo/capitals_and_countries%23map=0/4.2/180&color=continent

Follow that link and, after a short loading screen, you'll find yourself on a page that looks like this:

That's Datasette running the new datasette-maplibre plugin, loading up a database of GeoJSON shapes of countries and displaying both a combined map and individual boundary maps in a table.

Let's break down that URL to see what it's doing:

https://lite.datasette.io/
        ?install=datasette-maplibre
        &url=https://.../demo.db
        &metadata=https://.../metadata.yml
        #/demo/capitals_and_countries%23map=0/4.2/180&color=continent

The ?install=datasette-maplibre installs that additional plugin from PyPI. You can pass &install=... as many times as you like to load more plugins.

&url=https://.../demo.db loads that SQLite database from the provided URL. These URLs need to have open CORS headers - I host files like this in Gists, because they provide an easy way to get open CORS headers on a web-hosted file.

&metadata=https://.../metadata.yml loads this metadata.yml file. The metadata file adds HTML descriptions to various tables, and to the Datasette homepage. Visit that homepage here for a guided tour of the other features of that plugin, all defined in the metadata file.

#/demo/capitals_and_countries%23map=0/4.2/180&color=continent is a fragment hash that turns into a location within Datasette - here it's loading the /demo/capitals_and_countries SQL view, then appending another fragment hash to it (%23 is a URL-encoded #) which tells the map plugin to zoom to a certain location and to set the color of the shapes on the map based on the continent column in the data.

That URL is doing a lot of work! I wrote more about this trick for building URL-addressable software in URL-addressable Pyodide Python environments last year.

The full set of supported URL arguments is described in the Datasette Lite README.

I've already started using Datasette Lite as part of the Datasette development process. Here's a recent issue describing a pagination bug - I posted a comment there demonstrating the old, broken behavior and the new fix using links to Datasette Lite:

Demo of the bug: https://lite.datasette.io/?ref=1.0a42&sql=https://gist.github.com/simonw/75ececf61d50e6e8d50f0c150150ee81#/data/scores?_size=2&_sort=score - click next and the second page is empty.

Here's that same page with the bug fixed (running on 1.0a43): https://lite.datasette.io/?ref=1.0a43&sql=https://gist.github.com/simonw/75ececf61d50e6e8d50f0c150150ee81#/data/scores?_size=2&_sort=score

How this works, using service workers

Datasette Lite is not a new project. I launched the first version back in 2022, originally as a bit of a joke (running server-side apps in the browser is pretty funny) but one that quickly started proving its value.

The problem with that initial version is that it was a hack. It worked by running Datasette in a Pyodide web worker, simulating requests through that stack, then injecting the resulting HTML back into the top level page using innerHTML.

This worked for basic Datasette, but meant that any feature that used JavaScript failed to work, because script tags in innerHTML don't execute, and the web worker tricks it used failed to load additional JavaScript or CSS files.

The new version takes a completely different approach based on Service Workers. These allow JavaScript to intercept HTTP requests for new pages and resources and serve them from client-side code instead.

Datasette Lite registers a service worker for the entire lite.datasette.io domain. The parent page then creates an iframe that sends requests for Datasette pages to URLs that look like this:

/app/aa94e6851595/ # the homepage (HTML)
        /app/aa94e6851595/data/places # a table page (HTML)
        /app/aa94e6851595/-/static/navigation-search.js # (JavaScript)
        /app/aa94e6851595/-/static/app.css # (CSS)

Those are regular Datasette URLs, but with a /app/aa94e6851595/ prefix. What's that about?

The /app/<session>/ prefix is necessary because of multiple tabs.

Consider the URL above, which loads the demo instance with the datasette-maplibre plugin. That URL defines a full, custom Datasette instance. You might have that one running in a tab, then one of my other demo links running in another.

The service worker for lite.datasette.io is shared between all of those tabs. If it routed to a single instance of Datasette then every tab would share that underlying instance, no matter what plugins or other settings their URL attempted to configure.

Instead, the parent page generates a random session ID and uses it as a prefix for all of the subsequent hidden asset and page loads. The service worker can then use that session ID to route those requests back through the parent page to a web worker running a dedicated Datasette instance for that particular session.

(We still need a web worker because Pyodide in a service worker would not be able to maintain state beyond around 30 seconds, depending on the browser. There are a lot of moving parts here!)

I had Claude Fable 5.2 generate several SVG diagrams to help explain this. Here's my favorite of those, now embedded in the Datasette Lite README:

This system started life back in May as an AI research spike generated using Claude Opus 4.8. It wasn't until November (and Claude Fable 5.2) that I felt familiar enough with how it all works to confidently ship it to production!

Bonus feature: pick your version of SQLite

I added this feature last night as an off-shoot of investigating a potential bug in SQLite.

Datasette is meant to work against any released version of SQLite since 3.25 (released in September 2018). There have been 87 further releases since then.

Being able to fire up Datasette against a specific version of SQLite is really useful for demonstrating new SQLite features and debugging weird issues.

In the past I've used various tricks to get different SQLite versions running with Python on my Mac, but it's not a trivial process.

WebAssembly is perfect for this. I can load up a custom SQLite build entirely in my browser, test it there, then discard it when I close my tab.

datasette/pysqlite3-wasm-wheels is my new repository which contains WebAssembly compiled Python wheels for pysqlite3 for 163 different SQLite versions. Each version gets a file with a name like this:

pysqlite3-0.6.2-3.54.1-cp314-cp314-pyemscripten_2026_0_wasm32.whl

That's for SQLite 3.54.1, the most recent version.

Datasette Lite now takes a special ?sqlite= URL parameter, which will accept a version number like 3.54.1, resolve the path to the corresponding wheel file, then fetch that wheel and install it into the Pyodide environment and configure Datasette to use it.

Once I'd built the wheels, I decided to have Claude Fable 5.2 build me [this bonus tool](https://datasette.github.io/pysqlite3-wasm-wheels/?versions=3.54.1,3.54.0&sql=select+json_object(%27a%27%2C+(select+json_array(1%29%29%29) for comparing a SQL query across any selected versions of SQLite. Here's an example showing how select json_object('a', (select json_array(1))) differs between SQLite 3.54.0 and 3.54.1:

This should work for every other Python app, too

Nothing about how Datasette Lite works is unique to Datasette. Almost any Python application should be able to pull the same trick - running entirely in the browser using WebAssembly and Pyodide, as a cheap way to provide preview environments, demonstrate features, and recreate bugs.

C and Rust extensions used to be a blocker for this kind of thing, but any good coding agent can compile those to Pyodide-compatible WebAssembly now. You can even publish them to PyPI as of PEP 783 in April 2026.

One catch is databases. SQLite is no problem at all, but running PostgreSQL or MySQL in WebAssembly, while possible, is still a path less trodden.

I'd love to see WebAssembly preview environments like these become a common pattern across the Python ecosystem.

For Hacker News: Full server-side Datasette Python app in the browser with service workers

A bug fix release for LLM, mainly to cover a problem with the most recent Homebrew package of the software.

Homebrew now ships the latest SQLite, 3.54.1, which includes a fix that broke LLM's logging code.

Short version: in SQLite 3.54.0 the following SQL:

select json_object('a', (select json_array(1)))

Returns this:

{"a":[1]}

But in 3.54.1 the same query returns this:

{"a":"[1]"}

According to D. Richard Hipp:

That was a bug fix. Per the documentation, (SELECT json_array(...)) returns SQL text, not JSON. Hence the 3.54.1 behavior is correct and 3.54.0 was a bug.

The workaround looks like this:

select json_object('a', json((select json_array(1))))

item.title: datasette 1.0a43
item.content:encoded:
Release: datasette 1.0a43

I've been leaning hard into Claude Fable 5.2 to help knock things off the 1.0 milestone, which is now 53% complete.

The biggest 1.0 item in this release is streaming support for output renderers - the built-in TSV and CSV export mechanisms now use this as well, and plugins can register themselves as capable of streaming every row in a table in one go via the new Response.stream() method.

There are a couple of security fixes, one of which I deemed deserving of a GitHub advisory: private stored queries could be exposed, granting access to the title and SQL of the query (but not allowing that query to be executed).

There are dozens of smaller improvements. The row page JSON representation finally has a design suitable for 1.0. A new <datasette-copy-button> Web Component provides copy-schema in various places. JSON in columns on the row page can be pretty-printed. There's a new DatasetteModal.confirm() JavaScript utility method. Plus dozens of bug fixes, including contributions by Zihan Dai, Peter Olkhovets, Ilya Khalafi, and Ankita Advitot.

The feature I'm most excited about is a pretty tiny one: I've added CSS multi-page view transitions to Datasette! Here's the commit - key CSS is as follows:

/* Enable cross-document view transitions,
           for anyone without prefers-reduced-motion */
        @media (prefers-reduced-motion: no-preference) {
        @view-transition {
        navigation: auto;
        }
        }
        /* .facet-results should morph from old position to new */
        html:active-view-transition .content > .facet-results {
        view-transition-name: facet-results;
        }
        /* So should a .table-wrapper, provided it contains .rows-and-columns */
        html:active-view-transition .table-wrapper:has(> table.rows-and-columns) {
        view-transition-name: rows-table;
        }

With that in place, navigations within Datasette - still staunchly a multi-page application - feel more like an SPA. This works on Safari and Chrome at the moment and I believe supports for Firefox is due to land in Firefox 162 on December 8th 2026 (seeing as they are no longer feature-flagged in Firefox Nightly.)

This release adds support for OpenAI-compatible endpoints, so you can configure Datasette to use an LLM hosted anywhere that talks the OpenAI pseudo-standard web protocol.

This means that if you're running local models with LM Studio or Ollama or llama.cpp (which just hit v1.0.0) you can run Datasette via uvx like this:

wget https://datasette.io/content.db
        
        uvx --with datasette-agent datasette \
        --root --secret 1 \
        -s plugins.datasette-llm.default_model '{
            "model": "lmstudio-qwen",
            "model_name": "qwen/qwen3.8-27b",
            "api_base": "http://localhost:1234/v1"
          }' content.db

And you'll get a local server running a Datasette Agent instance powered by your local model!

Release: datasette-leaflet 0.3

OpenStreetMap have a very reasonable policy that hits to their hosted tile server should send a referrer header. Datasette table pages used the Referrer-Policy: no-referrer HTTP header, causing plugins that loaded tiles from OpenStreetMap to violate that policy.

datasette-leaflet is the plugin that loads a bundled Leaflet so other Datasette plugins can depend on it. It now sets the referrer policy on the tile requests themselves to strict-origin-when-cross-origin, passing the host but not the full path to the page.

item.content:encoded:
Release: llm-gemini 0.37

Google launched Gemini 4 Hydrogen today - the lowest cost member of the Gemini 4 family.

It's actually not too far off the price of its much bigger siblings, Carbon and Argon. I'm finding Gemini 4's pricing really confusing. Here's the pricing scheme:

Model Dates Input ($/M) Cached input Output
Gemini 4 Carbon Through Nov 30, 2026 $2.00 $0.10 $10.00
From Dec 1, 2026 $4.00 $0.20 $20.00
Gemini 4 Argon Through Nov 30, 2026 $2.00 $0.10 $10.00
From Dec 1, 2026 $4.00 $0.20 $20.00
Gemini 4 Hydrogen   $1.50 $0.075 $7.50

Carbon and Argon are the same price, and both are scheduled to double in price on December 1st. If they're the same price, why have two different models? Google says that Argon "delivers Gemini 4 intelligence with faster responses and lower token spend per turn compared to Gemini 4 Carbon" - so it may be priced the same, but it will use less tokens per task.

Hydrogen, supposedly the cheap model, is currently only a 25% discount on its more capable peers. The Hydrogen price will make more sense after December 1st, when it will represent a 75% discount. It's still considerably more expensive than Claude Haiku 5.5 and GPT-6 Luna - they're both $0.10/$0.50, so Hydrogen is 15x that.

I had Hydrogen generate some pelicans. Here's a full comparison grid showing the pelicans for all three members of the Gemini 4 family at their three supported effort levels:

Considering how close they are in price, the difference in pelican quality for Hydrogen is quite stark.

Here's how Google describe Hydrogen's intended position in their mix of models:

In real-world software development, while teams rely on frontier models like Carbon and Argon for deep architectural judgment when designing systems or untangling subtle bugs, they still need a fast, disciplined execution model for writing code, running tests, and verifying changes. Hydrogen is built to stand on its own as a model for everyday work — or to pair with Carbon and Argon as the high-efficiency execution engine in multi-model workflows.

Most notably, Hydrogen is the new free tier model, and is the model that will power AI features in Google Search.

Gemini Decisions API

Google join Jev and OpenAI in the decision model category with "Gemini Decision 1". This new model API is almost identical to Jev: it supports the same three types of questions (yes/no, choice, and rubric-scoring) and even reuses Jev's term "Noul" for a yes/no question.

It's priced the same as the GPT-6 Luna decision model: 10 cents per million input tokens, and output is free. Jev remains the cheapest of the three, at 4.2 cents per million.

Jev is text (and JSON) only. OpenAI can handle text and images. Gemini Decision 1 is fully multi-model: it covers text, images, audio, video, and PDFs.

I tested it against video by passing these questions to it along with my Yonkers stomping robot video file:

dragon: Does this video have a dragon in it?
        robot: Does this video have a robot in it?
        france: Is this video set in France?

item.title: Anthropic's IPO roadshow video
item.content:encoded:
Anthropic's IPO roadshow video

Anthropic kicked off their IPO roadshow yesterday, and their roadshow video has some previously unreleased information about how their business works.

The section on "Approach to compute" with co-founder Tom Brown is particularly interesting, describing how Anthropic train and serve Claude across AWS Trainium, Google TPUs, NVIDIA GPUs, and AMD GPUs.

I'm not sure why there's no official video transcript, but here's one that I extracted using MacWhisper. Highlights below:

We train and serve Claude now across all four major chip families. That's only possible because early on we made an unconventional bet on a multi-chip strategy. At the time, many people thought that running AI models on different chips wasn't worth the effort. Each chip needs its own tailored software stack and inference stack, which is expensive and difficult to build. We've now been doing it for years, and we've gotten incredibly good at it. [...]

As an example, this year, we started working with AMD GPUs for the first time. In the past, bringing on a new chip platform took dozens of engineers months of work This time, we had Mythos try it out. It got Claude running on AMD in just three days, with basically no human intervention. Claude ported or wrote almost 100% of the kernels. [...]

The second driver of our compute advantage is our rate of discovery of compute multipliers. We focus on total effective compute, which is the multiplicative product of physical capacity times the compute multipliers that we discover. Each one we discover makes our pool of total effective compute bigger. For example, say you need 100 units of compute to train a model of a certain intelligence. A 4x compute multiplier means you can use 25 units of compute to train the exact same model. Or you can use those hundred physical units to train an even more intelligent model that would have previously required 400 units.

Compute multipliers create a competitive advantage for us that's hard to replicate. They build on each other. Each new multiplier we discover has a positive effect on the multipliers before it. They stack. We believe that this can accelerate even further as we approach recursive self-improvement. Claude will be able to discover compute multipliers entirely by itself, allowing the number of compute multipliers to grow faster and faster.

We got a hint at Anthropic's multi-chip strategy last September in their postmortem of three recent issues, where they described bugs that affected just their TPU deployments.

item.title: Introducing Our Smallest, Most Efficient Model: Muse Ember
item.content:encoded:
Introducing Our Smallest, Most Efficient Model: Muse Ember

Meta AI just launched their entry in the Claude Haiku/GPT Luna category: Muse Ember, which they describe as:

[...] our smallest and most efficient model designed for complex reasoning execution and the work agents repeat all day: tool calls, coding subtasks, routing, extraction, and long document parsing.

For shorter prompts it's priced the same as GPT-6 Luna and Claude Haiku 5.5 - both are $0.10/million input tokens and $0.50/million output. Today's other big model release, Claude Fable 5.2, is 80x that price at $8/$40.

The pricing is a little less straightforward as prompts get longer, though. Luna, Ember, and Haiku all support up to a million input tokens, but they also all have a threshold after which the price goes up. Taking that threshold into account Ember is priced between the two others:

Model Prompt size Input ($/M) Cached input Output
GPT-6 Luna ≤272k $0.10 $0.01 $0.50
>272k $0.20 $0.02 $0.75
Muse Ember 1.0 ≤200k $0.10 $0.004 $0.50
>200k $0.30 $0.012 $1.50
Claude Haiku 5.5 ≤100k $0.10 $0.01 $0.50
>100k $0.50 $0.05 $2.50

But comparing price-per-token doesn't really make sense these days, when reasoning tokens mean that different models might use dramatically different numbers of tokens to solve the same problem.

For that, one measure that's useful is the Artificial Analysis.

And even more useful than that is their Intelligence Index vs. Cost per Task chart, which shows the following for those three models:

The Muse Ember models sit right on that Pareto line - the line at which you can only improve one dimension by giving up another. Meta call this out in their announcement:

It also sits on the efficiency frontier of the full Artificial Analysis leaderboard: no model scores higher for less per task.

(That grey dot on the Pareto line in the middle of the green area is GPT-6.1 Terra (low) - clearly I should be paying more attention to the Terra family!)

Muse Ember has six reasoning levels - minimal, low, medium, high, xhigh, and max - so I rendered six pelicans riding bicycles. The "high" reasoning level failed to return a full SVG, and the other SVGs were surprising in that the reasoning level didn't cleanly map to the visual quality of the response.

Here's the "max" one, but the others are worth a look too:

The Ember pelicans are comparable in quality to those I got from Muse Wonder, which is 40x the price of Muse Ember.

item.title: Quoting Prompting Claude Fable 5.2
item.content:encoded:
Claude Fable 5.2 pays close attention to who owns the code it works on. In Anthropic’s testing on small coding tasks, the model tended to add to the existing structure when the prompt said nothing about ownership or presented the code base as someone else’s, even when that duplicated existing code. When the prompt said the code base was the model’s own, it often consolidated duplicated code and sometimes made related fixes without being asked.

If you want the model to improve the structure as it works, say that the code is its own:

You are the owner and long-term maintainer of this codebase, and its design is up to you.

The ownership sentence makes the model much more likely to consolidate duplicated code into one shared function. In Anthropic’s testing on small coding tasks, the model consolidated duplicated code in under 10 percent of runs without the sentence and in about 75 percent of runs with it.

— Prompting Claude Fable 5.2, Anthropic documentation
